justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable baseline with modest drift upward across horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 566 was anchored heavily on recent observed values and short-term momentum, assuming little deviation from the prevailing trend. The slight upward drift to 568 at one week and 572 at one month reflects a gentle underlying trend assumption — essentially that whatever process is generating these values has a small positive drift baked in, compounded over time. None of the horizons show dramatic movement because the baseline signal didn't suggest any imminent structural break or sharp reversal.

The confidence interval widths expand progressively across horizons in a fairly standard way. At one day, the interval is tight (549–583) because there's limited time for the process to deviate from its current trajectory, and short-term noise tends to be mean-reverting. By one month, the interval widens considerably (515–630) to reflect accumulated uncertainty — each additional day introduces fresh randomness that compounds, and over a month there's meaningful probability of drift, regime shifts, or exogenous shocks that are impossible to anticipate from near-term data alone. The widening also reflects model uncertainty: the further out you forecast, the less confident you can be that the same dynamics governing today will persist.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wider intervals. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a policy change, a demand surge, or a structural shift in the underlying series — could push values well above 630 over the monthly horizon. On the downside, a sudden reversal, correction, or negative shock could breach the lower bound. The one-day interval is most vulnerable to data surprises or sharp discontinuities that weren't visible in recent history. Thin tails in the stated intervals mean roughly one-in-ten outcomes should fall outside them by construction, so tail events are not just possible but expected with some regularity across repeated forecasts of this type.
